text:
Citation:

Volzhenin v.
Haile

Date:

20011116

2001 BCSC 1591

Docket:

B972767

Registry:  Vancouver

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

BETWEEN:

VLADIMIR VOLZHENIN

PLAINTIFF

AND:

BRUK TEKABE HAILE

DEFENDANT

REASONS FOR JUDGMENT

OF THE

HONOURABLE MR. JUSTICE THACKRAY

Counsel for the Plaintiff:

A.E.
Thomas

C.
Rizzo

Counsel for the Defendant:

G.L.R.
Ritchey

D.A.
Joyce

Dates and Place of Trial:

October
15—19,

22—26,
2001

Vancouver,
BC

[
1
]

The plaintiff was involved in a motor vehicle
accident on March 18, 1997.  Liability for the accident is admitted by the
defendant.  The plaintiff was injured but the extent of the injuries is in
question.  This makes relevant the personality of the plaintiff as well as his
physical and mental condition before the accident.  Fundamental thereto is the
issue of his credibility in that the treating doctors and those retained for
legal purposes all relied upon what they were told by Mr. Volzhenin.

[
2
]

As much as I am able I will chronologically
summarize the testimony and documentary evidence as to Mr. Volzhenin’s history
before the accident.

1966 - 1993

[
3
]

Mr. Volzhenin was born in Vladivostok on
November 6, 1966.  He obtained the equivalent of a Canadian high school
graduation in Russia and attended the Far East State University.  He graduated
in 1990 with a diploma as a geophysicist.  His average grade was B plus.  He
defected from the crew of a “scientific ship” into Vancouver in 1991.  He
testified that he thought his “life was in danger” in Russia.  Mr. Volzhenin
suggested that this was because he is, by “nationality”, not religion, a Jew.

[
4
]

Mr. Volzhenin testified that he was in good
health when he arrived in Canada.  He said that he had to pass strenuous
medical examinations in order to be accepted as a crewman on a Russian Ship.
Mr. Volzhenin attended English language courses at the Jewish Community Centre
in 1991 and 1992.  After that he attended the Western Canada International
College where he took intermediate English.

[
5
]

The first medical information available to the
Court is a referral to the Burrard Physiotherapy Associates by Dr. W. Ciszak in
May 1992.  Dr. Ciszak considered a diagnosis of chondromalacia of the right
knee.  The physiotherapist recorded that while playing soccer the plaintiff had
adducted his right knee.  She noted that a player landed on his lower leg and
that “getting up from chair is painful, stiff” and that “kneeling is painful.”
She considered meniscus damage.

[
6
]

Mr. Volzhenin had some restrictions as to
employment in Canada because of his immigration status.  He said that he was
“not allowed to work by the Immigration Department.”  However, he went into the
import/export business.  In his examination for discovery he deposed that
commencing in 1992 he worked for a friend in a trade company in Seattle.  He
also attended the West Canada College in 1992-93 and took a network
administration course in Burnaby at the Greater Regional Technical College.

[
7
]

Dr. Bennett’s excellent medical chart on Mr.
Volzhenin gives a detailed picture.  The first recorded visit was to
Dr. Orrin Webber, at the same office, in January 1993.  The next visit was
to Dr. Webber in July for a rash.

[
8
]

On July 14 Mr. Volzhenin and his fiancé, Rozalia
Novikova, had an “incident” at the Canada/U.S. border.  The plaintiff narrated
details of this to many doctors who recorded it in their records.  Mr.
Volzhenin testified that he was physically abused by R.C.M.P. officers.  He
said that he was grabbed by the neck, thrown to the floor and hurt his hand,
nose, forehead, right knee and mid-back and lost consciousness.  He was taken
to the Peace Arch Hospital.

[
9
]

The Peace Arch Hospital records note the chief
complaint was of an injury to the back and a laceration to the eye.
Mr. Volzhenin complained of “pain, back; pain groin.”  A physician
recorded that Mr. Volzhenin was complaining of low back pain radiating into his
right leg and right knee that “worsened during altercation tonight with
police.”  On examination he found a left scoliosis curve, a very tender right
sacroiliac joint, “SLR positive on right” and a leg length discrepancy.  X-rays
of the lumbar spine were reported as normal.  The doctor diagnosed a right
sacroiliac strain.  He understood that Mr. Volzhenin was to be deported to
Russia “probably tomorrow” and said that he should see a doctor on arrival in
Russia.  The plaintiff was not deported but married Ms. Novikova the next day.

[
10
]

On July 26 the plaintiff saw Dr. Bennett regarding the rash and a
feeling that he had reduced vision in the left eye.  A referral to an ophthalmologist
was arranged.  Dr. Garfinkle reported “no evidence of trauma” although there
was such a complaint.  Dr. Bennett did not see the plaintiff again until
September 21 at which time he complained of sneezing, nasal obstruction, head
pain and “forgetful since accident Jul/93-own language.”  A referral was
arranged to a neurologist.

[
11
]

The neurologist, Dr. A.J. Prout, reported on October 28, 1993, that
Mr. Volzhenin complained of headaches and “words finding difficulties.”  Dr.
Prout noted a “flat effect” and diagnosed depression.  He set out in detail the
narrative given to him as to the border incident.

[
12
]

Mr. Volzhenin made a claim under the
Criminal Injury
Compensation Act
in which he listed his injuries as “Back, leg, head,
(concussion), skin irritation aggravated, emotional trauma.”  On February 2,
1996, he wrote to the Criminal Injury Section and said that the injuries that
he received “… still going.  As a result I cannot work and live normal life.”
He asked that the case proceed more quickly.  He wrote again on February 29 and
outlined his financial problems in that his expenses were exceeding his
unemployment cheque.

[
13
]

In December 1993 Dr. Bennett recorded that the plaintiff’s low back
pain had improved considerably but that he still required physiotherapy.
Further, he stated that “he still forgets words from time to time.”

1994

[
14
]

In early 1994 x-rays were taken of Mr. Volzhenin’s lumbar spine.  No
abnormality was seen.  However, he continued to make complaints of low back
pain.  In May Dr. Bennett noted that he had “pain for about ten months” and
suggested a diagnoses of coccydynia.  An x-ray of the coccyx was reported as
normal.  Dr. Bennett referred Mr. Volzhenin to Dr. Libuse Tyhurst, a
psychiatrist.  Mr. Volzhenin continued his visits to Dr. Bennett complaining of
tension headaches, neck pain and upper back pain.

[
15
]

In October 1994 Mr. Volzhenin had redness and swelling of the left
elbow and numbness in the left ulnar nerve.  Electromyographic studies were
normal and the report suggested that the “numbness in the hands sounds more in
the ulnar distribution” and that the left elbow pain sounded suggestive of
bursitis.

[
16
]

In November Dr. Bennett received a consultation report from Dr.
Tyhurst.  She reported that she was seeing Mr. Volzhenin and his wife “at
less frequent intervals”.  She outlined the alleged circumstances of the border
incident that, in her opinion, left them with “clinical evidence of strongly
suppressed anger.”  Dr. Tyhurst said that Mr. Volzhenin was ”working
through the process of recovery from post-traumatic neurosis.”

[
17
]

In 1994 or 1995 he took computer courses at the Greater Regional
Technical College and became a landed immigrant.

1995

[
18
]

On January 16, 1995, Mr. Volzhenin complained to Dr. Bennett
that his left knee “gave way”.  Dr. Bennett noted that Mr. Volzhenin “has had a
number of musculoskeletal problems which have failed either to be well
understood or relieved.”  X-rays revealed “an old osteochondal fracture with
resultant osteochondritis dessecans.”

[
19
]

Dr. Bennett received a consultation report from Dr. Tyhurst
dated January 21, 1995.  She had been seeing Mr. and Ms. Volzhenin
separately to follow up “their gradual recovery from Post-Traumatic State.”
She noted that they did “not support each other” and that they were “compulsively
striving for academic achievement, which is clearly not only compensatory for
their sense of personal failure, but also tends to turn into mutual
competition.”  She was told by Mr. Volzhenin that he could not afford the
$300 fee attendant to obtain landed immigrant status.  She said that she would
recommend a $300 loan to the plaintiff but that “the recent malfunction and
intense pain in his left knee, which will require surgery, is greatly
contributing to his sense of helplessness.”

[
20
]

Dr. S. Horlick, orthopaedic surgeon, reported on the knee problem
and operated upon it in January, 1995. Mr. Volzhenin testified that in 1995,
just after the knee operation, two hooligans came into his home and wanted
information about the whereabouts of certain persons.  On a subsequent visit
these men brandished a gun and a knife and “they beat me up, cut my arm and
tried to scare me.”  He said that he received a small cut on the right side of
his face and attended at the Vancouver General Hospital.

[
21
]

Mr. Volzhenin had an infection in the area of the knee surgery and
had a skin rash for which he attended on Dr. Bennett in early 1995.  Dr.
Bennett referred Mr. Volzhenin to Dr. Vaclav Hyrman, a psychiatrist.  Dr.
Hyrman saw Mr. Volzhenin for the first time on March 1, 1995.  His understanding
was that the main problem was a post-traumatic stress syndrome suffered by the
plaintiff’s wife.  His clinical notes record a visit on June 23, 1995, with a
notation about the plaintiff’s wife and about some eye problem.

[
22
]

He saw Mr. Volzhenin three more times in 1995 but in his
medical-legal report he does not say anything about those visits.  His clinical
notes are generally indecipherable and extremely brief.  In testimony Dr.
Hyrman acknowledged his sparse charting.

[
23
]

On March 27, 1995, Mr. Volzhenin attended upon Dr. Webber
complaining of back pain.  Dr. Webber noted that Mr. Volzhenin had been
complaining of back pain at about the “T3 level for one year.”  There were also
complaints of a skin rash.  Dr. Webber said he would send a note to Human Resources
regarding a need for ongoing medication.

[
24
]

On May 1, 1995, Mr. Volzhenin attended upon Dr. Bennett and told him
that he had a “visit from the Russian Mafia.”  As a result he had a
“superficial laceration over the right forearm” and was unable to fully extend
or abduct his fingers.  However, the next entry in Dr. Bennett’s records is of
an x-ray report on December 2, 1995, of the left knee which showed “no
significant current abnormality.”  Dr. Bennett’s office examination “showed
nothing” and he referred the plaintiff to Dr. Horlick.

[
25
]

On December 27, 1995, Dr. Webber reported as follows:

Long complex story with language
problems-apparently has not been able to work as computer repairman since Nov.
15 due to L knee, L ankle, and R upper leg and back pain.  Form done for
insurance, to reassess with RDB with Dr. Horlick report.  Little to find on
exam of painful areas, well muscled, no evident pain at present.

[
26
]

The plaintiff’s income tax returns for 1991 to 1994 inclusive show
no income other than social assistance.  The amount of social assistance was
$6,425 in 1992, $9,702 in 1993 and $3,028 in 1994.  The statement of claim
describes Mr. Volzhenin as “a self employed natural healer.”  He testified
that in Russia people felt that he could heal them of bodily complaints.  In
Canada he pursued this and he testified that he had income from this in 1993.
In a statement given to I.C.B.C. on April 8, 1997, he said:

I work as a natural healer and I have my own
list of patients.  These patients are referred to me by word of mouth.  I use
natural methods to heal.  I am unlicensed.  I usually attend my
patient/clients’ houses to treat them.  I usually work on 2 to 4 patients per
month and I work on each patient 1 to 3 hours per week.  I generate
approximately 24 hours per month working on my patients.  This is a rough
estimate.  I charge between $120.00 to $300.00/hour.  This rate depends on each
case I work with.  I usually make between $4 - $5,000.00/month.

[
27
]

In cross-examination he amended the above statement.  Whereas in the
statement he said, “I usually work on 2 to 4 patients per month”, he amended
this to read “I use (sic) to work on 2 to 4 patients per month.”  In his
examination for discovery he deposed that he “worked on his own” as a
naturopath, that he got paid “from time to time” and that he did this
continuously from “about age ten … until the date of the accident.”

[
28
]

Mr. Volzhenin did not at any time declare income from natural
healing for tax purposes.  In re-examination he testified that he did not think
the income was taxable.  In response to questions from the Court the plaintiff
said that maybe he was going to give the money back to those that he treated
with natural healing and therefore he did not think that he had to declare it.
He thought he had read something to this effect in a book.

[
29
]

For the taxation year 1995 Mr. Volzhenin did not file a tax return
however he worked at Morgan Power Apparatus (Can.) Ltd. doing heavy machinery
work from April 22 to 28, 1995 and earned $599; worked for Pan Tech Systems
Inc. from May to July 1995 doing computer repairs and earned $ 5,525; worked at
Contractors’ Network Corp. in August 1995 as an independent consultant and
earned $1,750 and worked for Mountain Systems Corporation from September 1,
1995 to November 15, 1995 and earned $5,943.

[
30
]

In his Court testimony Mr. Volzhenin indicated that the Mountain
Systems Corporation job was his last employment until August of 1996 because he
had been told, presumably by people from Social Assistance, that he had “to
correct [his] health.”  He then referred to his back which he testified became
a problem in “about November ’95.”  He was also having a problem with his left
knee.

[
31
]

Unemployment insurance records signed by the plaintiff in November
1995 record that he was “no longer working” because of a shortage of work.
Further, that he was unable to work from July 13, 1993, until January 30, 1995,
because of medical reasons.

[
32
]

The Human Resources Department wrote the plaintiff a letter dated
April 17, 1996, regarding unemployment insurance.  This was responded to in a
letter dated August 9, 1996, written by his wife although she did not identify
herself as such.  She wrote over the signature “Rozalia Novikova, Project
Co-ordinator.”  She said that the plaintiff “stopped volunteering due to his
health problem in November 1995.”  She stated that he “had never been paid for
his volunteer work.”  Mr. Volzhenin also wrote to the Department and said that
he had never been paid and that he had volunteered until November 1995 at which
time he “got problem with health.”

[
33
]

Mr. Volzhenin and his wife initiated Human HiTec Assist  Society.
He described this as a non-profit society to help people adapt to a new
culture.  A component of this was the recycling of used computers.  He
testified that there was no “pay” from this but that income was anticipated
after it became better established.

[
34
]

The plaintiff served a one month practicum at Xerox in 1995.  Mr.
Volzhenin testified that he “tried” to get geophysicist certification in Canada
and that he is still “hoping” to get certification in Canada as an ecologist.
However, he is not able to obtain papers from his schools in Russia attesting
to his education.

[
35
]

In a letter dated August 9, 1996, which the plaintiff testified was
“ordered” by him but written by his wife, it is stated that Mr. Volzhenin “has
been employed by Human HiTec Assist since 15 January 1994 as a computer
specialist.  This is a full-time position” and that he was earning $900 a
week.  She said that his “earning in 1995 were approximately $46,800.”

1996

[
36
]

Mr. Volzhenin kept up his regular visits to Dr. Bennett’s office in
1996.  On his fourth visit of 1996, which was on February 1, Dr. Glenda Bennion
referred Mr. Volzhenin to “Ferdinand Knobloch’ with a diagnoses of “Anxiety”.
In March Dr. Bennett saw the plaintiff on two occasions for complaints of back
pain and on one occasion for anxiety.  He referred his patient to Dr. Nairn
Stewart, a physical medicine and rehabilitation specialist.

[
37
]

Mr. Volzhenin first saw Dr. Stewart on March 18, 1996.  She reported
that he was not working and had developed low back pain in October 1995.  He
had pain and numbness in his legs, sleep disturbance and limited activity
tolerance.  On examination his low back movements were limited and there was
sensory impairment over the L5 nerve root distribution.  X-rays revealed
degenerative changes at the T12 and L1 levels.  He reported that his low back
pain “subsequently settled” but he then began having more problems with his
thoracic spine and with chest pain.  Dr. Stewart referred him to a
rheumatologist, Dr. G. Reid.

[
38
]

On April 11, 1996, the plaintiff visited Dr. Bennett with complaints
about his back pain.  In the same month Dr. Stewart again saw the plaintiff.
At that time his left foot was less painful, his left knee had started clicking
again, his right leg pain was persisting and his left leg was feeling a bit
weak.  On May 10 he visited Dr. Bennett with back pain complaints and on May 23
he complained to Dr. Stewart that his left arm occasionally felt numb and he
had constant pain from the chest through to the upper back, but that his knees,
while still painful, were less of a problem.

[
39
]

On June 17, 1996, Mr. Volzhenin visited Dr. Stewart with complaints
of a poor sleep pattern, headaches, a locking left elbow, chest pain and neck
discomfort.  The plaintiff had two further visits to Dr. Bennett in June
regarding his back and a further consultation with him in July at which time
there was a referral to a Dr. Reid.  Dr. Reid wrote a lengthy consultation
report in which he said that Mr. Volzhenin’s “history and physical examination
suggest that [t]his man has mechanical back pain.”  He recommended that Mr.
Volzhenin continue with his exercise program.

[
40
]

In August Mr. Volzhenin visited Dr. Bennett with complaints of right
hip joint pain of two weeks duration.  On September 11, 1996, Mr. Volzhenin saw
a doctor in Dr. Bennett’s office and complained of an unsteady feeling for
a week associated with nausea and mild lower abdominal discomfort.

[
41
]

Dr. Stewart’s medical-legal report states that in September 1996 Mr.
Volzhenin was still experiencing back pain and limitation of his activity
tolerance.  He reported a work trial but his sleep problem “interfered with
this, as he was unable to get up to go to work on time.”  Dr. Stewart said that
it was evident “that he had experienced a good deal of anxiety in relation to
an altercation that he had had with police at the Canada/US border in 1993.”
Mr. Volzhenin made a number of physical complaints that Dr. Stewart thought
were related to anxiety.

[
42
]

Dr. Stewart’s clinical notes of the visit on September 26, 1996,
contain a significant account from the plaintiff as to his perceived
condition.  In digest they speak of reported nervousness and “feels afraid of
some things, feels danger, not safety, like something will happen.”  Mr.
Volzhenin told Dr. Stewart that he thought his night fears might be
subconsciously related to the border incident.  The notes record that Mr.
Volzhenin was not working however began a work trial “but on day 3 & 4 could
not wake up on time & was late.  Explained his situation – no longer going
but may again in future.  Sedentary work – lots of sitting hard for him.”

[
43
]

Dr. Stewart reported to Dr. Bennett in a letter dated September 26,
1996.  She said as follows:

When I saw him today, Vladimir’s chief
complaint was of ongoing difficulty sleeping.  He reported that he begins
feeling very nervous at about 11:00 pm and feels a sense of impending danger.
He lies awake until at least 1:00 am and not infrequently until 5:00 am.  Once
he falls asleep, he sleeps anywhere from 5-10 hours but this is
non-restorative.  His sleep pattern interfered with a voluntary work trial, as
on the third and fourth days after beginning work, he overslept and was late.
When he explained the situation to his prospective employer, it was suggested
that he not return until the sleep problem had been overcome.  In any case, the
work was sedentary and he had difficulty sitting for the required period of
time.

[
44
]

The clinical records record that upon awakening Mr. Volzhenin
felt pain in his hands and feet and weakness.  Most of this was reported to
resolve in about ninety minutes but that he had minor discomfort that continued
all day.  He reported that his neck was “somewhat better but still a bit uncomfortable
looking to the left.”   He said that his back was still painful but that his
knee was better.

[
45
]

Dr. Stewart then gives more details as to the physical complaints
before outlining some of his perceived social problems.  These included
incidents with the police and with “bad guys” from Russia.  Mr. Volzhenin
informed Dr. Stewart that he had a criminal injury claim from the border
incident and that he would provide her with the claim number.  He apparently
wanted a “letter to be written requesting funding for bio[feedback]” in that
his “present problems with sleep related to anxiety arising out of that
incident.”

[
46
]

Dr. Stewart conducted a physical examination and got the
“impression” that the plaintiff had an “ongoing mechanical low back problem,
many somatic complaints - ?anxiety.”  In cross-examination Dr. Stewart said
that on the basis of what she was told at this visit Mr. Volzhenin would have
had difficulty working.  She said that his condition was such that it was a
barrier to work but she would have predicted physical improvement and a return
to work.  She further agreed that from May to September 1996 Mr. Volzhenin’s
mental and physical condition deteriorated resulting in his inability to work
by September.

[
47
]

On September 30, 1996, Mr. Volzhenin appeared without an
appointment.  He brought in his Criminal Compensation information.  He had
“taken a little run” but was unable to feel his right leg and suddenly there
was a sharp pain “like cut through bone (patella) L knee” and he fell to the
ground.  His back was also sore.

[
48
]

On October 3, 1996, Dr. Bennett referred Mr. Volzhenin to Dr. Philip
H. Adilman, a psychiatrist.  On October 11 Dr. Webber filled out forms for
insurance for Mr. Volzhenin following further complaints of back pain and
insomnia.  In November Mr. Volzhenin had Dr. Bennett complete forms regarding
his disability and he also enquired as to who he was to see “next week
concerning his back.”  Dr. Bennett told him it would be Dr. Shamburger.

[
49
]

Dr. Adilman saw Mr. Volzhenin on November 19, 1996.  In his report
Dr. Adilman stated that the referral was for “ongoing anxiety, sleeplessness,
and vague somatic complaints including headaches, backache and generalised
pain.”  Mr. Volzhenin told Dr. Adilman that “he has been doing computer
work but is now not working. … He says that he cannot work at the present time
due to ‘physical condition, spine and leg – my disc, back pain’.”

[
50
]

Dr. Adilman reported that many financial problems and problems
between Mr. Volzhenin and his wife dated from the 1993 incident at the border.
He said that Mr. Volzhenin was fearful of the police and stayed awake most of
the night.  Dr. Adilman recorded that Mr. Volzhenin told him that there
was a big problem with the marriage and that he was suspicious regarding
authorities.  His “impression” was that the plaintiff was not suffering from a
major mental disorder but “could well be suffering the effects of a post
traumatic stress syndrome.”

[
51
]

On November 26, 1996, Dr. Bennett again saw Mr. Volzhenin and
recorded that the plaintiff was to see Dr. Adilman “again today.”  Dr. Bennett
said that there was “apparently some concern about a brain injury because of
Vladmir’s behavioural problems.”  He went to see “people in New Westminster –
some society to do with brain injuries.”  In a “counselling visit” on November
29 Dr. Bennett noted that the plaintiff  “continues to have problems of
insomnia.”  In 1996 Mr. Volzhenin had twenty visits to his family
practitioner’s office.

[
52
]

Dr. Hyrman had an office visit with Mr. Volzhenin on December 23,
1996.  In his report Dr. Hyrman said that the plaintiff was still having
problems with his spine and headaches.  He also complained of “speaking”
difficulties that he attributed to the border incident.  He further complained
of sleeping problems that included “seeing frightening creatures.”  Mr.
Volzhenin had reduced his physical activity because of a loss of feeling in his
right leg.

[
53
]

Dr. Hyrman concluded that Mr. Volzhenin was preoccupied with his
somatic symptoms and that his “main problems were moderate anxiety, depression
and insomnia.”

1997

[
54
]

On January 7 he paid another visit to Dr. Hyrman accompanied by his
wife who “complained that he changes every few weeks, that he has headaches, he
forgets what he went to a grocery store for, he walks and talks in his sleep.”
In his medical-legal report Dr. Hyrman recorded that he next saw
Mr. Volzhenin after the accident, on May 16, 1997.  He said that he had
seen him “only a few months before that and at that time he was quite bright
and energetic.”

[
55
]

In cross-examination Dr. Hyrman’s records were reviewed with him and
he agreed that the plaintiff’s physical and mental condition were worse in 1996
than in 1995.  He further agreed that depression as described in DSM IV, the
bible of psychiatry, would not permit an observation of “bright and
energetic.”  He then acknowledged that such a description was an error on his
part in that he had diagnosed the plaintiff as being depressed.  Dr. Hyrman
reflected that not only was his note taking poor but his memory was obviously the
same.

[
56
]

In early January 1997 Mr. Volzhenin attended upon Dr. Bennett
complaining about pain in his left knee that he said he had re-injured.  On
January 20 Mr. Volzhenin had an electroencephalogram at the Vancouver General
Hospital.  It was reported as “normal for a drowsy patient.”  On January 21 Mr.
Volzhenin again saw Dr. Adilman.  Dr. Adilman’s clinical notes commence by
saying that “He is not working, not on social assistance but does get cash
money from time to time.  He is vague about where his income comes from.”  Dr.
Adilman recorded that the plaintiff “continues to complain of muscular problems
and Dr. Bennett will refer him to physio.  He had an EEG yesterday.”  Mr.
Volzhenin spoke at length to Dr. Adilman about the border incident.

[
57
]

On February 8, 1997, Dr. Tyhurst wrote a letter to Dr. Hyrman.
Dr. Tyhurst said that she was “Rozalia Novikova’s” doctor and that she was
“very glad indeed that Vladimir agreed to see you and that he will continue to
do so if we so recommend.”  Dr. Tyhurst then detailed the dynamics of Ms.
Novikova’s personality and compared this to that of Mr. Volzhenin who
“does not excel at manipulation” resulting in a “constant stream of simmering
anger that he feels against anyone in authority or power.”  Because of his wife’s
manipulation the plaintiff “is operating in his every day life with simmering
rage, which he is unable to express.”

[
58
]

Dr. Tyhurst said that Mr. Volzhenin had a number of symptoms,
several of which were a direct result of the border incident “yet not of such
intensity as they are portrayed by him.”  She agreed that Mr. Volzhenin was
“suffering from Post-Traumatic Stress Syndrome, with pre-existing personality
deficiencies.”  She suggested that when the plaintiff came to a realization of
the “facts of the relationship [with his wife] he will probably act out
aggressively or become clinically more depressed.”

[
59
]

On February 18, 1997, Mr. Volzhenin attended upon Dr. Adilman.  The
plaintiff reported that things were “going quite well” and then spoke at length
about the border incident.  He told Dr. Adilman that he was healthier before he
was “beat up.”

[
60
]

On March 11, 1997, Mr. Volzhenin again visited Dr. Adilman.  Dr.
Adilman made several notes about Mr. Volzhenin’s comments and Dr. Adilman said
that Mr. Volzhenin was “narcissistic and a bit of a know-it–all.”  Mr.
Volzhenin said that he had sent his wife to Russia to be away from the Russian
mafia in Vancouver.  Then he added: “I often wonder where he gets his money.
He says he does computer work and gets consultation fees.”

[
61
]

Counsel for the plaintiff cross-examined Dr. Adilman on the issue of
Mr. Volzhenin’s employment and source of funds.  Dr. Adilman testified that the
plaintiff was “very vague about his work … he was strange … he was very vague …

DISCUSSION

[
82
]

The 1993 border incident was traumatic, particularly mentally, for
the plaintiff.  In 1993 he attended Dr. Bennett six times and also had a
neurological consultation.  Mr. Volzhenin initiated a criminal
compensation application. In 1994 Mr. Volzhenin attended upon Dr Bennett twelve
times.  He had numerous complaints of back pain.  Dr. Bennett had concerns
about Mr. Volzhenin’s mental health and referred him to Dr. L. Tyhurst, a
psychiatrist.  She diagnosed a post-traumatic stress syndrome.

[
83
]

Mr. Volzhenin had many physical and mental complaints in 1995.  He
had back problems and he underwent surgery on his knee.  Dr. Bennett referred
Mr. Volzhenin to Dr. Hyrman, a psychiatrist.  Some form of assault occurred
involving the Russian Mafia.  Mr. Volzhenin’s wife moved to Richmond.
Mr. Volzhenin had several different jobs during the year and as well was
involved in a society with social motives.  Mr. Volzhenin had thirteen
visits to Dr. Bennett in 1995 and as well had psychiatric consultations with
Dr. Tyhurst and Dr. Adilman.  In order to have Mr. Volzhenin assessed by a
doctor culturally in keeping with Mr. Volzhenin, Dr. Bennett referred Mr. Volzhenin
to Dr. Hyrman, a psychiatrist.  A diagnosis of depression was made.  In
December Dr. Webber reported that Mr. Volzhenin was unable to work due to a
variety of physical problems.

[
84
]

In 1996 Mr. Volzhenin continued to speak to the doctors about the
border incident and to pursue, with their help, his claim for compensation.
Dr. Bennett referred Mr. Volzhenin to specialists in physical and psychiatric
medicine because he did not feel that he “even came close to coming up with a
diagnosis.” Dr. Bennett testified that he did not diagnose Mr. Volzhenin
as a malingerer but he never did get a “picture” of his patient.

[
85
]

It was acknowledged by Dr. Barbara Allan, a neurologist, during her
cross-examination, that a marriage marred by discord is a factor to consider in
assessing the mental health of a party to the marriage.  Consequently, the
marital situation of the plaintiff has significance in this action.

[
86
]

My impression of Mr. Volzhenin’s pre-accident history is of a person
with mental and personality problems and of a person with many complaints, to
his doctors, of physical problems.  The question is whether he was fantasizing
them or inventing them for compensatory reasons.  In coming to a decision on
this question, the credibility of Mr. Volzhenin is a critical factor.

[
87
]

While medical records say that Mr. Volzhenin was unable to work in
1996, the fact is that he was working, although he defined it as a training
program.  However, when asked about his athletic activities in the year or two
before the accident, he said that “right before the accident I don’t do much
activity because I was working but I like to run and walk around my places.”  I
have no difficulty in concluding that Mr. Volzhenin was “working” in the
ordinary sense of that word.

[
88
]

When the plaintiff was asked on his examination for discovery if
between September 1996 and March 1997 he ever “told people that [he] was not
working”, he answered: “Well, I think so.”  He was then asked if he ever told
people that he was not “capable of working because of your physical condition”
and he answered, “It’s possible.”

[
89
]

In cross-examination a note made by Dr. Stewart on September 26,
1996, was read to the plaintiff.  In it she stated that Mr. Volzhenin was “not
working” and that he was “no longer going” to the work trial.  He was asked if
he told Dr. Stewart that he was not working and if he told her that the work
trial lasted three or four days “but didn’t work out.”  His answer was “yes”.
Mr. Volzhenin conceded that he told Dr. Adilman on November 26, 1996, that he
could not do computer work because of his physical condition with his spine and
because of leg and back pain.  He also told Dr. Bennett on that date that there
was concern that he had suffered a brain injury.

[
90
]

Mr. Volzhenin declared no income from natural healing but his
statement to ICBC claims he made “between $4 - $5,000/month.”  He compounded
the problem by testifying that he did not think he had to declare it if he was
going to return it to his patients.  During his examination in chief I
interjected to ask why the issue of the plaintiff’s psychic healing was
relevant.  Counsel for the plaintiff answered that “he was earning income from
it.”  I then asked the plaintiff if he “was earning income from that?”  Mr.
Volzhenin answered: “I received money.”  He said that he did not spend it on
himself and that he did not “really” keep records.  He stated that “most of the

[
91
]

In cross-examination Mr. Volzhenin agreed that he gave a statement
to ICBC after the accident that he “usually” worked on “two to four patients
per month” at a charge of “between $120 and $300 per hour.”  In the statement

[
92
]

Mr. Volzhenin filed tax returns for the years 1991 to 1994, years in
which he claimed no income.  However, in 1995, a year in which he held several
paying jobs, he failed to file tax returns.  He suggested in his testimony that
because tax returns are not required in Russia he did not know that he had to
file one in Canada.

[
93
]

The testimony of lay witnesses is in startling contrast to the
picture that Mr. Volzhenin was giving of himself to his doctors.  All lay
witnesses saw Mr. Volzhenin as a physically healthy individual.  The evidence
of Mr. LeMoine and Mr. Mutual is particularly descriptive.  They saw no
indications that he was in any physical discomfort, much less under any
physical disability.

[
94
]

This, in itself, raises a significant question as to the veracity of
Mr. Volzhenin’s complaints to his doctors.  If his credibility was intact
elsewhere it might be that some other explanation would be feasible.  However,
even Mr. Volzhenin, in giving his testimony, did not attempt to explain the
many contradictions that he had to know were forthcoming in the evidence.

[
95
]

In an application for a MasterCard in October, 1999, Mr. Volzhenin
stated that his “annual salary” was $46,800 from Human HiTec.  Mr. Volzhenin’s
explanation for this was that HiTec owed him that amount of money.  He was
involved in the preparation of a letter in 1996 stating that his earnings in
1995 were $46,800 from HiTec.  This letter was in support of a credit
application to Toyota.  In response to questions as to how he could consider
the money from HiTec income for credit purposes but not for tax purposes, Mr.
Volzhenin did not offer any explanation.

[
96
]

When Mr. Volzhenin was asked if he “made a claim for money under the
Criminal Injury Compensation system”, he said, “I don’t make a claim for
money.  I ask for, how you call it, justice.”  The claim was disallowed and the
plaintiff appealed.  In February 1996 Mr. Volzhenin wrote two letters asking
that the appeal be expedited because he was in an “emergency situation” in that
he had been unemployed and was having “a problem with a collection agency.”  It
sounds to me like a claim for money.

[
97
]

I have detailed some examples of evidence that causes significant
concern as to his credibility.  In his written submission counsel for the
defendant listed seventeen examples of what he termed to be the plaintiff’s
“deceit”.  I do not intend to repeat those or to comment on each individually.
Suffice to say I find weight in the submission.

[
98
]

Apart from these examples of Mr. Volzhenin’s credibility problems,
there is other evidence that at least required some explanation, which was not
forthcoming.  Mr. Volzhenin testified that he “tried to see Dr. Bennett” after

24, 1997, and referred him to an opthamologist.  Dr. Bennett had office visits

[
99
]

This next visit took place on November 21, 1997.  Dr. Bennett
reported: “General appearance normal, head and neck normal, lungs normal, CVS
normal.”  Mr. Volzhenin saw Dr. Bennett regularly throughout 1998 and
1999.  The last recorded visit was on March 29, 2000.  In testifying
Mr. Volzhenin said that Dr. Bennett is still his “general doctor though I
don’t see him very often … I go more often to the North Shore.”  If he was
making reference to some doctor on the North Shore, no doctor was identified
nor did any family practitioner subsequent to Dr. Bennett give evidence.

[
100
]

Considering Mr. Volzhenin’s acute memory of
injuries, doctors, marital history, employment history etc., it is not
consistent that he cannot remember seeing Dr. Bennett innumerable times
throughout 1997, 1998, 1999 and into 2000.

[
101
]

Another instance of testimony that does not
reflect favourably upon Mr. Volzhenin concerns headaches.  Mr. Volzhenin
testified that he has had headaches since the accident but that he did not “have
such headaches” before the accident.  He said that he “might have from time to
time headaches, maybe, but I don’t exactly remember.”  The clinical records of
Dr. Bennett and Dr. Prout, neurologist, dating from as early as September 21,
1993, contain complaints of headaches diagnosed variously as preorbital and
anxiety type headaches.  On November 26, 1996, he attended upon Dr. Adilman
with “vague somatic complaints including headaches.”  Dr. Adilman said
that “Vladimir has problems with his back and he has headaches.”

[
102
]

On December 23, 1996, he made complaints to
Dr. Hyrman of frequent headaches.  On January 7, 1997, only three months

he went to a grocery store for.”

[
103
]

Forgetfulness is pleaded as an injury although
forgetfulness was a complaint from the time of the border incident.  It has to
be considered whether the lack of memory  about pre-accident headaches is as a
result of forgetfulness. If forgetfulness is in any way related to memory, he

which he attended.  He said his son was born on March 25, 1989 “at 10:15.”  He
remembered that his second child was born on May 2, 1997, “about two months

[
104
]

Much the same type of testimony came from the
plaintiff regarding neck problems.  “Injury to the neck” is pleaded and Mr.

[
105
]

On May 23, 1996, Dr. Stewart diagnosed a
decreased range of motion in the cervical spine, with lateral flexion to the

[
106
]

Counsel for the plaintiff conceded that
Mr. Volzhenin’s lack of credibility had been established.

[
107
]

In considering the plaintiff’s motives and
credibility, I have not restricted myself to the evidence of Mr. Volzhenin’s
pre-accident history.  I have reviewed all of the evidence in this case and can
find nothing to salvage Mr. Volzhenin’s credibility.  I am satisfied that
Mr. Volzhenin was on a financial mission to which end he deceived his
doctors and, when it was to his perceived advantage, he deceived others who
were either entitled to or sought information regarding his finances.  This conclusion
is reinforced by Mr. Volzhenin’s trial testimony wherein he avoided the truth
and added another layer of lies.

[
108
]

It remains to consider the post motor vehicle
accident evidence, apply to it this credibility finding and determine what
