126
]

Dr. Stewart wrote three medical-legal reports.
In the first she recorded that on May 12, 1997, the plaintiff had a “flat”
effect and “there was loss of his previous animation.”  General physical
examination was normal.  She diagnosed “soft tissue injury to his neck and left
shoulder, and of post concussion syndrome.”

[
127
]

Dr. Stewart next saw Mr. Volzhenin in early 1998
after his return from Russia.  She recorded that he “was feeling much better
physically” but “reported memory difficulties.  Dr. Stewart noted that he was
less articulate in English than prior to the accident “and it was becoming more
and more apparent that he had sustained a significant brain injury affecting
his language abilities and executive intellectual functions.”  An MRI brain
scan done on May 25 “showed no brain abnormality.”

[
128
]

Dr. Stewart, in the report dated October 8,
1999, wrote that she “last saw Mr. Volzhenin on August 26, 1998” but she said
that he “continues to suffer sequelae of the brain injury sustained in the
motor vehicle accident of March 18, 1997.”

[
129
]

The first time that Dr. Stewart saw the
plaintiff after August 26, 1998, was on May 15, 2000.  Mr. Volzhenin reported
that he was “much better – twice, three times better.”  He complained of sleep
problems and headaches and continued to have lapses of memory.  Dr. Stewart
noted that “he was well groomed and was dressed smartly in a suit.  He was
cheerful and joking.”

[
130
]

The only physical findings recorded in the
report are limitations in the range of lateral flexion of the cervical spine.
Dr. Stewart said “his former sense of humour was more evident than on other
visits since the motor vehicle accident; he indicated that this is largely
pretense, as others expect it of him.”  Cranial testing was largely negative
with the only positive sign being a decrease in the rate and rhythm of rapid
alternating movements in the left hand.”  Immediately upon noting these results
Dr. Stewart outlined the conclusions of Dr. Hyrman, Dr. Allan and of an
occupational therapist and then gave her “opinion”.

[
131
]

Her opinion was that Mr. Volzhenin “sustained a
significant brain injury, mild to moderate in severity” and has residual
cognitive, emotional and behavioural deficits.”

[
132
]

Dr. Stewart next saw Mr. Volzhenin on March 28,
2001.  In her report she detailed a trip that Mr. Volzhenin took to Russia from
August until November 2000.  She recorded that he told her that he had been
diagnosed with two medical problems while undergoing “investigations in
Leningrad and Vladivostok, and had some treatment in Vladivostok.”  He told
her, and she recorded, that the investigations included electroencephalograms
“which he was told showed evidence of damage to both sides of his brain.”  He
had with him several medical reports written in Russian and “one EEG
recording.”

Dr. S.D. Anderson

[
133
]

Dr. Anderson was retained by counsel for the
plaintiff to author an “independent psychiatric assessment.”  He interviewed
Mr. Volzhenin on May 1, 2000.  The interview lasted two and one half hours and
is detailed in the first twelve pages of Dr. Anderson’s report.  Dr. Anderson’s
report then reviews the reports of many of the doctors who gave evidence in the
trial as well as the psychological report of Dr. Schmidt, a psychologist.  He
noted that Dr. Schmidt did not think that Mr. Volzhenin had “any major
cognitive deficits” but qualified Dr. Schmidt’s conclusion by saying that
“executive functioning is difficult to assess with neuropsychological
testing.”  Dr. Anderson then reviewed the reports of community therapists
before stating his opinion.

[
134
]

He concluded that the evidence from “physicians
and other collateral sources is that Mr. Volzhenin has changed dramatically
following” the accident.  He then repeated Dr. Schmidt’s opinion and went
on to define executive functioning.  He said that it is the ability to
formulate goals, the ability to plan and achieve goals and the ability to carry
out plans effectively.  In Dr. Anderson’s opinion “there has not been any
significant impairment of Mr. Volzhenin’s actual intelligence, but instead
his executive functioning skills and thinking speed and efficiency have been
affected.”

[
135
]

Dr. Anderson concluded that Mr. Volzhenin’s
“preferred diagnosis would be personality change secondary to traumatic brain
injury. … It is unclear why Mr. Volzhenin has developed ongoing difficulties
following mild traumatic brain injury.”

[
136
]

Dr. Anderson explained in cross-examination that
there is no objective evidence that the plaintiff’s ongoing problems are from a
brain injury.  That is, there is nothing such as a CT scan or MRI.  He said
that he had to infer brain injury from the Glasgow Coma Scale, the loss of
consciousness and amnesia.  He explained, as did other doctors, that in at
least 90% of the cases of such an injury all problems will resolve.  Dr.
Anderson testified that Mr. Volzhenin has depressive symptoms but that these
are not major and “do not explain his cognitive problems.”

Dr. Barbara Allan

[
137
]

Dr. Allan, a well known and highly respected
neurologist, was retained by counsel for the plaintiff.  She saw the plaintiff
on March 23, 2000.  Her lengthy and detailed reports were filed as evidence and
as well Dr. Allan gave oral testimony.

[
138
]

Dr. Allan’s reports conclude that Mr. Volzhenin
“probably” had frontotemporal brain damage.  She said this in the context of
his writing being “suggestive but not diagnostic” of a “resolving language
disorder” and that this finding is “suggestive but not diagnostic of a left temporal
lobe abnormality.”  In cross-examination she conceded that the plaintiff’s
language difficulties are not diagnostic and that she relied largely on her own
findings.  She said that she had “suspicions” about brain damage and, as I
understand her opinion, she satisfied herself of this as much as she could by
language testing.  This included having the plaintiff write out certain
material.  Dr. Allan found Mr. Volzhenin’s writing to be messy with
“cross-outs” and that his grammar and spelling was not in keeping with a person
of his education.

[
139
]

Dr. Allan said that she would have liked to have
a psychologist do specific language testing.  In response to this Dr.
Wilkinson’s neuropsychological tests were brought to her attention.  Dr.
Wilkinson’s test results on language revealed that comprehension of complex
language was normal, that reading out loud was adequate and that sentence
writing was normal with well formed handwriting.

[
140
]

Dr. Allan responded by saying that she would
like to see the handwriting that Dr. Wilkinson obtained from the plaintiff as
well as examples of the plaintiff’s handwriting before the accident. This was
produced to her in the form of letters that Mr. Volzhenin wrote in 1996
regarding his criminal injury claim.  Dr. Allan said that they were “different”
from what she had obtained.  She said that there were no cross-outs in the 1996
letters and that they were “quite neat and well placed on the page.”

[
141
]

Dr. Allan agreed that there were no abnormal
findings in her neurological examination other than “language errors, apathy
and fatigue.”  She also agreed that his tiredness might have negatively
affected his language test.  She further testified that the plaintiff’s
language problem is not consistent with either malingering or depression and that
“it must be explained and I cannot explain it on the basis of depression.”

[
142
]

Dr. Allan was asked to assume that there were
pre-existing language problems.  She said if that is so then she is left only
with reports of executive function problems and a blow to the head as a
foundation for her opinion.  She conceded that she did not have a good
understanding of his pre-accident executive functioning.

Dr. Michael Jones

[
143
]

Dr. Jones is a neurologist.  He was retained by
counsel for the defendant.  He testified that whatever brain injury was
suffered by the plaintiff was “on the very mild end of the scale … such people
almost always recover within two to three months.”  In his report Dr. Jones
said that the plaintiff “is certainly a puzzle.”  Dr. Jones reviewed other
reports, noted the negative findings of Dr. Schmidt and of the findings at
Vancouver General Hospital on his admission following the motor vehicle
accident.  The resident doctor, Doctor Patterson commented that it was unclear
whether Mr. Volzhenin had suffered any unconsciousness.  The neurosurgeon, Dr.
Honey, who saw the plaintiff the day after the accident, said that there was
“no suggestion of a significant closed head injury.”

[
144
]

Dr. Jones’s examination revealed no damage to
the olfactory nerve.  This is significant in that loss of smell is common in
closed head injuries.  Dr. Jones testified that if there is significant brain
damage or if there is brain damage to the extent alleged in this case, the
olfactory nerve "goes”.

[
145
]

In his oral testimony Dr. Jones explained that
for there to be executive function problems requires damage to both frontal
lobes.  He said that memory problems do not arise from damage to one lobe
only.  Consequently, there would have to be diffuse damage to the plaintiff’s
brain and “scans do not support this.”  He testified that there was nothing
“subtle” about the alleged brain damage and said that if the plaintiff has what
he alleges by way of deficiencies “it would involve all of the brain … all but
the back part.”

[
146
]

In his report Dr. Jones said that he found the
plaintiff “odd and atypical for the type of complaints that he volunteers.”  In
testifying he said that the type of complaints voiced by the plaintiff, and he
listed them, “are not the things about which brain damaged people speak.”  He
said “you do not get the alleged problems with a mild brain injury.”  [I will
note here that this quotation, as with all others except those from Mr.
Volzhenin, for which there was a transcript of evidence, are from my bench
notes and might not be exact.]

DISCUSSION

[
147
]

The observations of Mr. Mutual and Mr. LeMoine,
while sporadic, indicate that Mr. Volzhenin’s work performance was
unsatisfactory after the motor vehicle accident.  However, their testimony
revealed that they were not acute observers of Mr. Volzhenin.  I also gained
the impression that they were “going to bat” for him in that he had done them a
great favour in the summer of 1996.

[
148
]

Mr. Triemstra met Mr. Volzhenin at ITV in April
1997 at which time Mr. Volzhenin was working sporadically.  He was not
impressed with the plaintiff’s work and found him disruptive at meetings.  Mr.
Sawyer first met Mr. Volzhenin in the spring of 1998 at ITV and described him
as a casual information technology worker.  He was also involved in the work trial
at which Mr. Volzhenin was unsuccessful.

[
149
]

While not answering the question as to “why”,
this evidence confirms that Mr. Volzhenin was not working at a satisfactory
level in the months after the accident and did not perform well at the work
trial.  His performance on the work trial has built in weaknesses in being used
as a yardstick.  Mr. Volzhenin was being tested and he knew why.  By that time
ITV was having serious business problems and its Vancouver operation was
considerably downsized.

[
150
]

Both Mr. Lobassov and Mr. Alexandrov saw a
difference in Mr. Volzenhin after the motor vehicle accident.  Their
observations were casual and sporadic and centred, for the most part, on his
physical condition.  Ms. MacDonald could not provide a pre and post accident comparison
in that she did not meet him until November 1997.  She socialized with him in
the sense of travelling with him on extensive trips but at home he generally
socialized with his many friends.  Ms. MacDonald did not observe emotional or
mental problems in Mr. Volzhenin but rather noted that he limped and twisted.

[
151
]

I expected Dr. Bennett to be able to give the
best before and after assessment of the plaintiff.  However, he could not
figure him out at either time and it was therefore left to his clinical records
to capture his findings.  His clinical records for October and November 1997
indicate, indeed diagnose, a healthy individual.  Dr. Bennett’s testimony that
his October assessment of a “virtually recovered” patient and his confirmation
of this in November by a “complete physical” is important evidence.

[
152
]

Dr. Stewart made findings of brain damage and
continuing sequalae but her opinions cannot be accepted without reservations.
Her medical examination of May 12, 1997, led only to a diagnosis of post concussion
syndrome and a soft tissue injury.  It was a year later that she next saw the
plaintiff.  He had just returned from Russia and was feeling much better
physically but reported memory difficulties.  On what seems to be extremely
scant evidence she said that “more and more” it was becoming apparent that
there was a significant brain injury.

[
153
]

More than another year passed before she again
saw Mr. Volzhenin but she found that he “continues to suffer sequlae of
the brain injury.”  After nearly another year Dr. Stewart again saw the
plaintiff and he reported that he was “much better” but complained of sleep
problems, headaches and lapses of memory.  However he was “cheerful and joking”
and, according to Dr. Stewart, evidenced  “his former sense of humour.”  Mr.
Volzhenin passed this off as being “largely pretense” as others expected it of
him.  This was quite a clever explanation, apparently accepted by Dr. Stewart.

[
154
]

Dr. Stewart’s examinations were largely negative
but she continued to find “a significant brain injury” with residual deficits.
It is apparent from her report that this is based to a great degree upon
opinions expressed by others who in turn were relying upon the truth of what
they were told by Mr. Volzhenin.  Indeed, in cross-examination, Dr. Stewart
conceded that her diagnosis was based upon self-reporting and that if that was
untruthful then the diagnosis is unreliable.  She agreed that in the absence of
objective evidence of the injuries the truth of the plaintiff’s self-reporting
is crucial.

[
155
]

Dr. Stewart’s report of March 28, 2001, gives me
particular concern.  The physical examination was unremarkable and the
neurological examination seemed to involve only word finding and expressive
language assessments.  Dr. Stewart detailed the opinions of others, many of
which had an untested basis.  Furthermore, each of them seemed to rely on the
other and in turn Dr. Stewart did likewise.  For instance, Dr. Stewart
relied upon a report from Ms. Ruby Schulstad to conclude that while the
plaintiff is “functioning reasonably well” and living independently in a suite,
“this is largely because of the support of his landlady and friends.”  This is
not evidence before the Court and indeed conflicts with the testimony of Ms.
MacDonald.

[
156
]

Dr. Stewart also referred to neuropsychological
testing done by Dr. J.P. Schmidt that “revealed weaknesses in mental efficiency
consistent with a brain injury”.  Dr. Schmidt apparently concluded that
the injury was mild and “did not show major cognitive deficits.”  Curiously, his
report is not in evidence.

[
157
]

The Court does have as evidence the report and
oral testimony of Dr. R.V. Wilkinson, also a neuropsychologist.  She found the
plaintiff’s “executive functions to be adequate.”  Her testing revealed the
plaintiff’s intellectual functions to be strong with his “weakest performances”
in “attention functions, but all other scores were high average to superior.”
She said that attention function problems arise with brain trauma in the early
months but that the “speed of processing improves and attention function
generally resolves.”

[
158
]

Dr. Wilkinson testified in cross-examination by
counsel for the plaintiff that the low scores of Mr. Volzhenin could arise from
a variety of factors including mood disorder, boredom, pre-existing attention
problems and motivation.  She found his motivation to be generally good but
noted that he “got bored with simple tests.”  She stated in reply to questions
from plaintiff’s counsel that the test results are inconsistent with the degree
of brain damage allegedly suffered by Mr. Volzhenin.

[
159
]

I want to make it clear that I am not being, and
I should not be taken to be, critical of Dr. Stewart.  She relied upon what she
was told and what others found on the same basis.  She testified that her
diagnoses was based partly on reports, partly on what she was told by Mr.
Volzhenin and partly on his apparent inability to communicate.  I am of the
opinion that the self-reporting and apparent language problems were fundamental
to her opinion.  Dr. Stewart acknowledged that the MRI report was that “the
intracranial contents were normal” and that there was “no MR evidence of
traumatic brain injury.”

[
160
]

In her report Dr. Stewart recorded opinions
expressed by Dr. Allan, Dr. Jung (who had spoken to the plaintiff’s former
employer), Mr. Nordin, vocational consultant, Dr. Yu, Dr. Anderson and Ms.
Russell, occupational therapist.  She then confirmed her earlier opinion of
brain damage and said that he is “incapable of coping without considerable
support in the community.”  I can see no sound basis for that opinion from Dr.
Stewart.

[
161
]

Dr. Stewart agreed that there was no hemosiderin
detection by the MRI.  Hemosiderin is a substance left by blood.  She said this
means that there is no evidence of scarring but that “it does not mean that
there was no trauma.” Dr. Michael Jones, neurologist, said that if there had
been tears in Mr. Volzhenin’s brain there would have been bleeding and if there
had been bleeding there would have been signs of hemosiderin.  He said that the
radiologist who assessed the MRI knew that he was dealing with an alleged
closed head injury and would pay particular attention to the matter of
hemosiderin.  Furthermore, there was no atrophy of the brain, that is,
shrinking.

[
162
]

In her report Dr. Allan said that the
frontotemporal abnormalities were “likely the result of diffuse axonal injury
as a result of shearing forces on the brain at impact.”

[
163
]

However, she agreed in cross-examination that if
there had been bleeding you would expect to find hemosiderin.  She said that
the lack of hemosiderin might be explained by accepting that there was no
bleeding but rather just stretching and swelling of the blood vessels “or maybe
there were just tiny tears that resolved by the time of the MRI.”  In
re-examination she seemed to back away from this latter conjecture in that she
noted that the MRI was done fourteen months after the accident “not two or
three years later.”

[
164
]

The point upon which her report was heavily
grounded was the language difficulty, particularly Mr. Volzhenin’s difficulties
with writing.  Dr. Allan saw a significant difference between the plaintiff
pre-accident writing and post-accident writing.  I do not.  They were both
messy, contained cross-outs and contained spelling and grammatical errors.  I
tend to the opinion that if Dr. Allan had had the pre-accident writing when she
did her testing, and had access to Dr. Wilkinson’s language tests results, that
her opinion might well have been different.

[
165
]

I also found the evidence regarding hemosiderin,
as given by several witnesses, including Dr. Allan, to establish that there was
probably no bleeding from or within the brain in the accident.  This left Dr.
Allan’s opinion based almost entirely upon her assessment of the plaintiff’s
language difficulties.

[
166
]

Dr. Stewart’s physical examination revealed only
some minor problems.  Neurologically, she noted “word finding and other
expressive language difficulties.”

[
167
]

In view of the lack of objective findings,
taking into consideration the importance of self-reporting to
Dr. Stewart’s opinion and recognizing that the plaintiff had problems with
language and words before the accident, I cannot without other compelling
evidence give much weight to Dr. Stewart’s opinions.

[
168
]

I felt particularly confident with Dr. Michael
Jones’s report and oral testimony.  He seemed less intimidated by the opinions
of others and secure in his own opinions.  It was at the end of his
cross-examination by counsel for the plaintiff that he gave answers that were
particularly compelling.  He said that atrophy of the brain would have shown in
the MRI if the alleged brain damage had occurred, that people do not get the
plaintiff’s alleged problems with a mild brain injury and that in his opinion
the plaintiff had a head injury, not brain damage.

[
169
]

I asked Dr. Anderson what he felt he could
contribute to this case that had not been covered by the other doctors,
particularly the psychiatrists.  He frankly conceded that he could contribute
very little.  He said “a lot of my opinion is based on what was said by Dr.
Hyrman.”  He testified that when he concluded in his report that
Mr. Volzhenin’s “executive functioning skills and thinking speed” have
been affected, he was simply repeating what had been said by Drs. Hyrman and
Stewart.

[
170
]

I found Dr. Anderson to be particularly frank
and refreshing.  He acknowledged that the more a psychiatrist sees a patient
the better will be the diagnosis.  He was referring here, of course, to the
fact that he only had one interview with the plaintiff.  He added that
“psychiatry is not a science, it is an art.”  When Dr. Anderson was asked in
cross-examination why Mr. Volzhenin has not recovered as do in excess of 90% of
people with mild brain injuries, he said that it is an “enigma” as to why Mr.
Volzhenin had personality changes after the accident.  Shortly thereafter he
said that Mr. Volzhenin is a “puzzle” and he was glad that it was the Court,
not him, that had to make the ultimate decision as to the injury and the cause
of Mr. Volzhenin’s alleged condition.

[
171
]

The Court has no evidence as to the medical
“investigations and treatment” that Mr. Volzhenin received in Russia.  The
plaintiff testified that he received treatment in Russia and he told many of
his local doctors the same thing.  He informed Dr. Yu that he had “manual
therapy” in Russia.  Dr. Stewart recorded in some detail what she was told in
this regard, including the plaintiff’s assertion that EEG’s in Russia showed
“damage to both sides of his brain.”  I do not know what effect this had upon
Dr. Stewart’s thinking, but the proffering of this information to her and not
to the Court makes what he told her suspect and added no strength to
Dr. Stewart’s opinion.

[
172
]

Counsel for the defendant submitted that there
are other “gaps in the evidence” that negatively affect the plaintiff’s
credibility as well as the foundation for his claim for both non-pecuniary and
loss of income awards.  He pointed out that people such as Ms. Volzhenin and
Mr. Olson, the plaintiff’s roommate, were not called to testify as to the
plaintiff’s condition before the accident.  He submitted that apart from
testimony as to Mr. Volzhenin’s ability to perform as an employee, there is no
evidence as to his “executive functioning” before the motor vehicle accident.

[
173
]

Defence counsel also noted that many of the
plaintiff’s medical and other experts relied upon reports that were not
tendered in evidence.  In particular, the neuropsychological report of Dr.
James Schmidt, referred to by many doctors including Drs. Stewart, Hyrman, Jung
and Allan.  Another problem created for Dr. Allan, not by her but for her, was
the failure to file in evidence the “speech-language assessment done in July,
1998” upon which she relied.

[
174
]

All of these points made by defence counsel
have, in my opinion, merit and none of them were answered in the plaintiff’s
case.

CONCLUSION
REGARDING BRAIN DAMAGE

[
175
]

Counsel for the plaintiff cited
Cloutier
v. Wong
, New Westminster Registry No. C890285,
[1991] B.C.J. No 3843
(Q.L.) (S.C.)
.  Therein I said that I posed the question as to whether the
plaintiff suffered organic brain damage only to say that it cannot be answered
“at least by me.”  I noted that there were “diametrically opposed opinions from
highly qualified and eminent medical doctors.”  I said that the question for
the Court to answer was whether organic brain damage had been proven on a
balance of probabilities.

[
176
]

One of the “eminent doctors” that gave an
opinion in that case was Dr. Hyrman.  Another was Dr. Vallance whose report was
filed in the case at bar.  The importance of a valid medical history was
emphasized in that case.  It was conceded that psychiatrists rely heavily
thereon.  Dr. Vallance said that “the history is the single most important
factor in coming to a diagnosis.”  There are, indeed, similarities between the
problems posed in that case and in the case at bar.

[
177
]

I agree with Dr. Jones who said “this is a
difficult case because of the diversity of opinions expressed.”  He was, of
course, speaking medically.  The task of the Court is somewhat different.  As I
indicated in
Cloutier
, it is not for the Court to express a
medical opinion.  The test is whether on a balance of probabilities the
plaintiff has established his case.  When I say “his case” I am referring to
brain damage which is what this case is really all about.  I find that he has
not.

[
178
]

Mr. Volzhenin deceived his medical advisors as
to his condition before the motor vehicle accident.  I have no reason to think
that he is not continuing to do so.  His motivation pre-accident was money
driven and he has not given the Court reason to think that this motivation is
not continuing or that his moral code has improved.

[
179
]

When the issue of the plaintiff’s credibility
was being considered by Dr. Anderson, he asked the Court “how could Mr.
Volzhenin pull the wool over so many doctors’ eyes?”.  Counsel for the plaintiff
in his submission used this to suggest that it is unlikely that his client
could do that.  I would not presume to answer that question but the length of
these reasons are as a result of the Court’s effort to explain why it believes
that he did.

[
180
]

Counsel for the defendant cited short passages
from two cases that he submitted are appropriate to apply to the case at bar.
I agree.  In
Butler v. Blaylock Estate
,
[1981] B.C.J. No. 31
(Q.L.)(S.C.)at paragraph 18
Chief Justice McEachern said as follows:

I am not stating any new principles when I
say that the Court should be exceedingly careful when there is little or no
objective evidence of continuing injury and when complaints of pain persist for
long periods extending beyond the normal or usual recovery period.

[
181
]

The other case cited to the Court is
Le v.
Milburn
,
[1987] B.C.J. No. 2690 (Q.L.)(S.C.) at page 1
wherein
Southin J. wrote:

When a litigant practices to deceive,
whether by deliberate falsehood or gross exaggeration, the court has much
difficulty in disentangling the truth from the web of deceit and exaggeration.
If, in the course of disentangling of the web, the court casts aside as untrue
something that was indeed true, the litigant has only himself or herself to
blame …

[
182
]

Counsel for the defendant put it this way:

… the evidence clearly establishes that
Mr. Volzhenin’s past is characterized by so much deception that it is
impossible to know what is the truth and what is fiction. …[K]eeping in  mind
that the plaintiff bears the onus of proving the claim on a balance of
probabilities, the other evidence that has been tendered simply leaves too many
questions unanswered.  Simply put, the difficulties facing the Court are the
fault of the plaintiff and no one else and, as such, … any doubts must be resolved
against the plaintiff.

[
183
]

The claim for brain damage of any more than a
transitory nature has not been established.  The claim for loss of income
earning capacity is dismissed.

INJURIES
SUSTAINED IN THE MOTOR VEHICLE ACCIDENT

[
184
]

Mr. Volzhenin was admitted to the Vancouver
General Hospital on March 18, 1997, and was discharged on March 22.  He had
sustained a blow to the left side of his head and exhibited bruises on the left
side of his head and face.  His jaw was injured.  Dr. W. Yu, orthopaedic surgeon,
from a review of the Vancouver General Hospital records, said in his
medical-legal report that he “believes” that Mr. Volzhenin sustained injuries
to the head, neck, back, left eye, left jaw, left hip and right knee.

[
185
]

Dr. Yu first saw Mr. Volzhenin on March 15,
2000.  He reported that the plaintiff’s “past health has been good.”  Dr. Yu
seemed to have a limited history of Mr. Volzhenin and I assume when speaking of
“past health” he was referring to pre-accident.

[
186
]

Dr. Yu reviewed x-rays of the plaintiff’s
cervical and lumbar spine taken on March 18, 1997.  He said they were normal.
He compared these to x-rays taken on March 14, 2000, which he said show
degeneration in the cervical spine.  He therefore concluded that this “dramatic
change can only be explained by the motor vehicle accident.”  Dr. Yu noted Mr.
Volzhenin “moved his neck freely during conversation.”

[
187
]

Dr. Yu recorded Mr. Volzhenin’s complaints of
pain including headaches, neck and “lower cervical pain most of the time”,
shoulder pain, left elbow pain, right wrist pain, numbness in his right hand,
low back pain, right knee pain, right ankle pain, right hip pain and right knee
pain.  However, his examination diagnosed a man “in good general condition”
with his “main orthopaedic injury” being his right knee.  Dr. Yu agreed in
cross-examination that his opinion could change if there was a previous right
knee problem.  Dr. Yu did not, apparently, know that there had been.

[
188
]

Dr. Yu acknowledged that he “believed what
Mr. Volzhenin told me.”  Mr. Volzhenin told him that his headaches and
left eye pain occurred for the first time after the motor vehicle accident.  He
told Dr. Yu that “everything was fine” before the accident.

[
189
]

Narrative accounts of the plaintiff’s injuries
run throughout the many medical reports filed in this action and in the
clinical records of some doctors.  Most of the injuries, after the initial
signs of trauma subsided, are evidenced by subjective complaints of pain,
weakness, numbness and fatigue.

[
190
]

Mr. Volzhenin’s oral testimony as to the state
of his health at the end of 1997 was that he had headaches almost daily, pain
in his neck, "cannot really move my head”, left shoulder pain, lower back
pain that limited walking, left elbow locking, numbness in hands, teeth and jaw
problems, poor appetite, a lack of energy and a lot of problems with dizziness
and nausea.

[
191
]

Mr. John Tai, a registered massage therapist,
was not called as a witness although his clinical notes were entered as an
exhibit.  Mr. Volzhenin first attended upon Mr. Tai on June 24, 1998, on a
referral by Dr. Bennett.  Dr. Bennett said that Mr. Volzhenin required
massage therapy “due to injuries sustained in a motor vehicle accident.”  He
said that the areas to work on were the neck, shoulders, upper and lower back,
hips, knees, legs and hands.  Mr. Tai also initiated massage on the plaintiff’s
head.   The massage seems to have encompassed almost every area of Mr.
Volzhenin’s body and extended to skin problems.

[
192
]

Dr. Bennett was not asked to comment upon his
referral for massage nor cross-examined as to whether the referral note was in
order to obtain insurance coverage or actually represented Dr. Bennett’s
opinion.  I am not going to elevate the note to a medical opinion from Dr.
Bennett.  This would be inconsistent with Dr. Bennett’s physical findings in
November 1997.  What the referral is consistent with is a “subluxation” in the
plaintiff’s right hip.  It is referred to in Dr. Bennett’s clinical note for
June 4, 1998.  It is also consistent with the Burrard Physiotherapy Associate
records of June 15, 1998, wherein it is stated that the plaintiff “felt like he
dislocated” his right hip “2 –3 weeks ago.”

[
193
]

If Dr. Bennett in any way associated the
referral to the motor vehicle accident, it had to be based upon the
self-reporting of Mr. Volzhenin.  There is so little credibility in that
reporting that the note, at most, can represent only a reflection of what Mr.
Volzhenin was claiming, not what he was actually suffering.

[
194
]

On December 12, 1998, Mr. Tai reported to
Dr. Bennett that Mr. Volzhenin “presents exceptional range of motion” but
that there was “muscle tension and that

guarding was palpated throughout his body.”  In March, 1999, Mr. Tai reported
to Dr. Bennett that the plaintiff would “benefit from continued sessions” but
that his “coverage” had ended.  The therapy appears to have ended on April 20,
1999.

[
195
]

The plaintiff testified that he now suffers
headaches, minor neck pain, left shoulder pain, low back pain, knee problems,
nausea, teeth and jaw problems.  Dental problems are outlined in reports from
Dr. Vitaly Pomeranets and Dr. John N. Nasedkin.

[
196
]

How much of his complaints are relative to
injuries from the accident is almost impossible to assess.  All of the medical
reports rely heavily on Mr. Volzhenin’s self-reporting.  The credibility issue
being what it is leaves the Court hobbled in its determination of what injuries
are associated with the accident, what complaints preceded the accident and
were either exacerbated by the accident.  As well, the Court must decide what
weight to give to the complaints, regardless of their cause.

[
197
]

While Mr. Volzhenin complains about physical
limitations, I do note that he apparently socializes to a great degree.  Ms.
MacDonald’s testimony suggests that he has a wide circle of friends and is out
of the house almost every day.  I also note that in 1997, shortly after the
accident, he travelled to Russia.  In 1999 he holidayed in Las Vegas and on a
separate occasion in San Francisco.  In 2000 the plaintiff visited Russia and
attempted to locate and visit his son.  In 2001 he again visited Russia.

[
198
]

I do not find these trips to be in keeping with
the plaintiff’s alleged pain and limitations.  While in the courtroom he was
continuously turning and stretching and rarely sat down.  He even stood while
giving evidence, having suggested that pain limited his ability to sit.  There
was no explanation offered by the plaintiff as to how he could sit for what
must have been many hours on his various plane trips.

[
199
]

I also have concerns about the alleged
investigations and treatment in Russia.  There is no admissible evidence before
the Court as to what treatment he had or for what.  I recognize that there
might be some hurdles to overcome in calling such evidence, but there was no
hint to the Court as to why the suggested extensive investigations and
treatment in Russia were not produced in evidence.

[
200
]

Counsel for the defendant accepts that there
were soft tissue injuries, teeth and jaw problems.  He submitted that the
extent of the soft tissue injuries is difficult to assess because of the lack
of credibility of the plaintiff and that it is curious that treatment for the
jaw problems has not taken place.  He acknowledges that the plaintiff sustained
a concussion but asserts that any effects therefrom were resolved “by October,
1997, at the latest.”  Mr. Ritchey suggested a non-pecuniary damage award of
between $20,000 and $30,000.  Counsel for the plaintiff did not propose any
figure for this narrowed range of injuries.

[
201
]

I set the figure for the non-pecuniary damages at
$30,000.

LOSS OF INCOME

[
202
]

Mr. William Mutual testified that as far as he
“could recall”, Mr. Volzhenin went on to a “kind of a cash basis” in 1997.
Until that time the plaintiff had been working at ITV but had not been paid.
Mr. Mutual said that “Mike Silva” was handling “all of the administrative
functions.”  Mr. Mutual testified that “Mike Silva offered him a full-time
salary in March of ’97” and that he had seen the records.  However, no such
records were produced in evidence.  There is no employment record, no record of
any payments to the plaintiff and no record of any employment contract.
Mr. Mutual explained this omission by saying that ITV had a poor
accountant.

[
203
]

Furthermore, Mr. Silva, who allegedly offered
the plaintiff a $40,000 job commencing on March 15, 1997, was not called as a
witness.

[
204
]

The plaintiff testified that he was on contract
for $1,000 a month from December 1996.  A letter dated February 1, 1997,
addressed “to whom it may concern” and signed by Mr. Mutual states that
the plaintiff was working “on a contract basis” commencing January 1, 1997.  It
states that the “payment, currently, is up to $1000.00/month.”  Mr. Mutual
testified that he could not remember signing the letter and added that “I guess
it is true.”

[
205
]

To further add to the contradictions, on January
21, 1997, Dr. Adilman recorded that the plaintiff told him that he was not
working.  In his statement to ICBC Mr. Volzhenin said nothing about working for
ITV.   The statement of claim describes the plaintiff as a “natural healer” and
makes no mention of his employment at ITV.

[
206
]

Counsel for the defendant submitted that “there
is simply no basis to award any wage loss.”  I understand that submission and
it has weight.  However, Mr. Mutual, while not a knowledgeable witness as to the
employment situation of Mr. Volzhenin, was aware of Mr. Volzhenin and
thought him capable of benefiting ITV as a paid employee.  I am going to give
the plaintiff the benefit of the doubt on this issue.

[
207
]

Dr. Wilkinson testified that if the plaintiff
was working at the time of the accident he would be “expected to be off for
some months.”  The maximum that this should have been, based on the evidence in
the case, is six months.  I will allow him the maximum and adopt the suggested
income of $40,000 a year.  This makes the award for loss of income $20,000.

CLAIMS FOR COST
OF FUTURE CARE AND SPECIAL DAMAGES

[
208
]

There will be no award for cost of future care
as such but there are some special damages claimed that might be said to fall
under that heading.  I will simply deal with them as special damages.

[
209
]

There is a claim for travel at one hundred
kilometres a month for 59 months at thirty cents a kilometre.  I will allow
twelve months for a total of $360.

[
210
]

There is a claim for massage therapy from Rick
Backman in the amount of $40.00.  His records indicate that the plaintiff
attended for massage in July and August, 1997.  This was on a referral from
either Dr. Bennett or Dr. Stewart.  This claim is allowed.  There is, however,
a letter from Mr. Backman that I find curious.  In it he said that he was
supplying his “complete clinical records dating from January 1, 1992.”  The
records put into evidence date from July 1997.

[
211
]

There is a claim for $970 for the massage
services of Mr. John Tai that commenced in June 1998.  The account, as with all
other accounts, was filed as an exhibit with an express reservation from
defence counsel with respect to causation.  I am not satisfied that the
referral was for injuries suffered in the motor vehicle accident, and the
account is not allowed.

[
212
]

An account from Burrard Physiotherapy Associates
is claimed at an amount of $680.  The physiotherapy appears to have commenced
on June 15, 1998.  That is the time of the hip dislocation.  The documents are
blank in the spaces for information as to “doctor” and “referral”.  Treatments
continued on a frequent basis until April 20, 1999.  As with Mr. Tai’s records,
the treatments appear to have been to almost every part of Mr. Volzhenin’s
body.  There is no substantiation that whatever treatments were given were as a
result of the motor vehicle accident.  The account is not allowed.

[
213
]

There are receipts for $160 from Jill
Orendorff, apparently a massage therapist, dated in the summer of 1999 and from
Gunnel Gavin, apparently a physiotherapist, dated in the summer of 1999 in the
amount of $60.  These are unexplained and are not allowed.

[
214
]

There is a claim for special damages for
chiropractic treatment.  Dr. Bennett said he did not refer Mr. Volzhenin to a
chiropractor.  The account for chiropractic services commences in March 1999.
The treatments concluded on August 5, 1999.  There was no evidence tendered as
to what services or treatment was provided.  This account is not allowed.

[
215
]

I will further note that there is a significant
overlap of physiotherapy, massage therapy and chiropractic treatments.  I
expect that it would be difficult to medically justify these three modalities
on an overlapping basis.  In any event, no attempt was made to do so.

[
216
]

The dental and orthodontic services claims will
be allowed.  I cannot ascertain from the material the amount.  If counsel
cannot agree upon it then they can come before me with submissions but I would
expect them to come to an agreement.

"A.D. Thackray, J."
